tool.name: json
tool.tagline: Encode and decode JSON, the lingua franca of APIs and config files
tool.description: The json module converts between Python objects and JSON text: dicts, lists, strings, numbers, booleans and None map onto JSON's types. It is how Python programs talk to web APIs, read configuration and store simple data. Beyond the basics it offers hooks to serialise custom types, decode into your own classes and control precision and formatting.

glossary.def: In JSON work: writing data out as JSON and then reading it back in. If you get back exactly what you started with, the data survived the round trip.
The programming language built into web browsers. JSON's look was borrowed from the way JavaScript writes data.
Python's type for exact decimal numbers, like Decimal("19.90"), from the decimal module. Unlike a float it keeps every digit you give it, which is why it's used for money.
A function you hand to a library so the library calls your code at a certain moment, for example each time it meets a value it can't handle by itself.
The error json.loads and json.load raise when the text isn't valid JSON. It records the line and column where reading went wrong.
The classes that do the work behind json.dumps and json.loads. You can make your own version (a subclass) to control how unusual values are written or read.
The part of Python's json module written in the C language for speed. It handles the common cases; some options make json fall back to slower code written in Python.
To print data laid out over several indented lines so people can read it easily, instead of squeezed onto one long line.
One agreed way of writing data as JSON, with key order, spacing and text encoding all fixed, so equal data always produces exactly the same bytes.
A short fingerprint computed from some bytes, such as SHA-256. The same bytes always give the same fingerprint, and changing even one byte gives a completely different one.
A code computed from some data and a secret key. Anyone can check it to prove who produced the data and that nobody changed it since.
Request for Comments: a numbered document published by the internet's standards bodies. Many formats and protocols are written down in one, like canonical JSON in RFC 8785.

concepts.name: dumps and loads
concepts.summary: Turn Python data into JSON text with json.dumps, and read JSON text back into Python data with json.loads.
concepts.why: Online services, settings files and many other programs exchange data as JSON, so reading and writing it is an everyday Python job.
concepts.body:
Programs often need to send data somewhere: save it in a file, or send it to another program over the internet. Python's dicts and lists only exist inside your running program, so first they must be turned into text. **JSON** is the most common text format for that, and it looks a lot like Python: `{"name": "Ann", "tags": ["a", "b"]}`.

JSON has a few kinds of values. An **object** is written in curly braces with `"key": value` pairs, just like a dict. An **array** is a list of values in square brackets, just like a Python list. The rest are strings, numbers, `true`, `false` and **null**, JSON's word for "no value", like Python's `None`.

Turning Python data into JSON text is called **serialising**. Reading JSON text and working out the data it describes is called **parsing**. The json module has one function for each:

- `json.dumps(obj)` ("dump string") serialises a Python value and returns a JSON `str`.
- `json.loads(text)` ("load string") parses JSON text and returns Python data. It also accepts `bytes`, so you can pass data straight from a file opened in binary mode or downloaded from the internet.

What `loads` gives back is made of ordinary Python types: dicts, lists, str, int, float, bool and None. There are no special JSON objects to learn; you use square brackets on the result like on any other dict or list.

Writing data out and reading it back, `json.loads(json.dumps(x))`, is called a **round trip**. For data made of these basic types you get back an equal value. The exceptions (tuples come back as lists, non-string keys become strings) are covered in the type-mapping lesson.

JSON's rules are stricter than Python's. Strings must use double quotes, a comma can't follow the last item, comments aren't allowed, and `true`/`false`/`null` are lowercase. So `str(my_dict)` does not give JSON: it gives `{'a': True}`, which a JSON parser rejects. Always produce JSON with `json.dumps`.
concepts.code:
import json

user = {"name": "Ann", "age": 31, "admin": False, "tags": ["a", "b"], "boss": None}
text = json.dumps(user)
print(text)
# {"name": "Ann", "age": 31, "admin": false, "tags": ["a", "b"], "boss": null}
print(type(text).__name__)          # str

data = json.loads('{"id": 7, "items": [1.5, 2], "ok": true}')
print(data["items"][0], data["ok"])  # 1.5 True
print(json.loads(b'[1, 2, 3]'))     # [1, 2, 3]

print(str({"a": True}))             # {'a': True}  -- not JSON!
takeaways: `dumps` turns Python data into a JSON string; `loads` parses one back into dicts, lists, strings and numbers
JSON uses double quotes and lowercase true/false/null
`str(dict)` is not JSON; always use `json.dumps`
pitfalls: Building JSON by hand with f-strings or `str()`; it breaks as soon as a value contains a quote mark.

quiz.q: What does json.dumps({'ok': True, 'v': None}) return?
quiz.explain: JSON uses double quotes and the literals true and null; dumps returns a str.

concepts.name: Reading and writing JSON files
concepts.summary: Save and load JSON files with json.dump and json.load, using an explicit UTF-8 encoding.
concepts.why: Settings, saved progress, test data and exported records are commonly stored in JSON files.
concepts.body:
For files, use the versions of the functions without the s:

- `json.dump(obj, f)` writes JSON to a file opened for writing.
- `json.load(f)` reads a whole file and parses it.

Open the file with `encoding="utf-8"`. JSON files are meant to be UTF-8, but `open()` without `encoding=` uses your computer's own default, which on Windows is often something else. Passing it every time makes the script work the same on every machine.

```python
with open("config.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    config = json.load(f)
```

A JSON file holds exactly **one** value, usually an object or an array. You can't add a second object to the end of the file and still load it with `json.load`. For a file you keep adding records to, such as a running history of events, use **JSON Lines** instead: a format with one complete JSON value on each line.

`json.load` reads the whole file into memory before parsing it. That's fine for settings and moderate amounts of data. For very large files, use JSON Lines and read one line at a time.

If people will read the file, pass `indent=2` so each value sits on its own indented line. If a crash halfway through writing would leave a broken file, write to a temporary file first and then swap it into place with `os.replace(temp_path, path)`, which replaces the old file in one step.
concepts.code:
import json

settings = {"theme": "dark", "font_size": 14, "recent": ["a.txt", "b.txt"]}

with open("settings.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(settings, f, indent=2)

with open("settings.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    loaded = json.load(f)

print(loaded == settings)     # True
print(loaded["recent"][-1])   # b.txt
print(open("settings.json", encoding="utf-8").read().splitlines()[1])
#   "theme": "dark",
takeaways: `json.dump`/`json.load` work on open files; `dumps`/`loads` on strings
Open JSON files with `encoding="utf-8"`
A JSON file holds one value; use JSON Lines for files you keep adding records to
pitfalls: Appending a second JSON object to an existing .json file, which makes it unparseable.

quiz.q: You call json.dump(record, f) twice on the same file opened in append mode ("a"), then json.load(f). What happens?
options: You get a list of both records
quiz.explain: Two JSON values one after the other are not one valid JSON document, so the parser complains about extra data after the first.

concepts.name: How Python types map to JSON
concepts.summary: Know exactly which Python types JSON supports, what they turn into, and what changes on a round trip.
concepts.why: Silent changes (tuples to lists, int keys to strings) cause confusing bugs after you save data and load it again.
concepts.body:
When `json.dumps` writes your data, it translates each Python type into a JSON one:

- `dict` → object, `list` and `tuple` → array
- `str` → string, `int` and `float` → number
- `True`/`False` → `true`/`false`, `None` → `null`

Reading with `json.loads` goes the other way. Arrays always become `list`. A number becomes an `int` if it has no decimal point and no exponent (like `1e2`, meaning 1 × 10²), otherwise a `float`.

What changes on a round trip:

- **Tuples come back as lists.**
- **Dict keys become strings.** JSON object keys must be strings, so `{1: "a"}` is written as `{"1": "a"}` and reads back with the key `"1"`. `True` and `None` keys become `"true"` and `"null"`. Tuple keys raise `TypeError` (unless you pass `skipkeys=True`, which silently drops them).
- If a dict has both `1` and `"1"` as keys, they become the same key in JSON and one of the values is lost.

Some types aren't supported at all: `set`, `bytes`, `datetime` (dates and times), **Decimal** (Python's exact decimal numbers, used for money) and objects of types you create yourself. Writing them raises `TypeError: Object of type set is not JSON serializable`. Later lessons show how to handle them.

Python's float has special values for "not a number" (**NaN**, what undefined maths like infinity minus infinity gives) and for infinity. `json.dumps` writes them as `NaN` and `Infinity`, but these are **not valid JSON**: careful JSON readers in other languages reject them.

Dict keys keep their order both ways.
takeaways: Tuples become lists and all dict keys become strings
Sets, bytes, datetime, Decimal and your own objects need explicit handling
NaN and Infinity are written out but are not valid JSON
pitfalls: Saving a dict with int keys and then looking them up with ints after loading.

quiz.q: cache = {200: 'OK'}; c2 = json.loads(json.dumps(cache)). What is c2.get(200)?
quiz.explain: The key was written as the string "200", so the int key 200 is not found and get returns None.

concepts.name: Pretty printing and compact output
concepts.summary: Control how JSON text looks with indent, sort_keys, separators and ensure_ascii, and pretty-print JSON files from the terminal.
concepts.why: Neatly laid-out JSON is easy for people to read and compare; compact JSON is smaller to store and send.
concepts.body:
`json.dumps` and `json.dump` take options that change how the text looks. Laying JSON out over indented lines so people can read it is called **pretty-printing**.

- `indent=2` pretty-prints, indenting each nested level by 2 spaces (it also accepts a string like `"\t"` for tabs). The default, `None`, puts everything on one line.
- `sort_keys=True` puts object keys in alphabetical order, so the same data always gives the same text. That's handy when comparing two versions of a file or checking output in tests.
- `separators=(",", ":")` removes the spaces after commas and colons for the most compact form. The default is `(", ", ": ")`, or `(",", ": ")` when `indent` is set.

By default, any character outside **ASCII** (the basic set of English letters, digits and punctuation) is written as an escape code: `"é"` becomes `"\u00e9"`. That is valid JSON but hard to read. `ensure_ascii=False` writes such characters as they are; then make sure the file is opened with `encoding="utf-8"`.

From the terminal, `python -m json.tool` checks that a file is valid JSON and prints it pretty-printed:

```bash
python -m json.tool --sort-keys settings.json
```

Other settings you can add: `--indent 4`, `--compact` for one line, and `--json-lines` for JSON Lines files (one JSON value on each line).

Formatting never changes the data, only spaces, line breaks and key order. Any JSON parser reads all of these versions the same way.
takeaways: `indent` pretty-prints; `separators=(',', ':')` gives the most compact form
`sort_keys=True` makes the output the same every time, for comparing and testing
`ensure_ascii=False` keeps accented and non-English letters readable; pair it with UTF-8 files

quiz.q: Which option makes two equal dicts with different insertion orders produce identical JSON text?
quiz.explain: sort_keys orders object keys alphabetically, removing insertion-order differences.

concepts.name: Handling invalid JSON
concepts.summary: Catch json.JSONDecodeError, report where parsing failed, and check that the decoded data has the shape you expect.
concepts.why: Input from users, files and other programs is regularly broken or not what you expected.
concepts.body:
`json.loads` and `json.load` raise **json.JSONDecodeError** when the text isn't valid JSON. It's a subclass of `ValueError` with useful attributes:

- `e.msg` the reason, e.g. `"Expecting value"` or `"Illegal trailing comma before end of object"` (3.13 wording)
- `e.lineno`, `e.colno` and `e.pos` (character position) for pointing at the problem
- `e.doc` the whole input

Common causes: an empty string, a trailing comma, single quotes, comments, or a web page where JSON was expected. The last one happens when your program downloads data from a web service and the server has a problem: instead of JSON it may send back nothing, or an error page written in **HTML** (the language web pages are written in). Check that the download succeeded before parsing it.

Parsing successfully doesn't mean the data is right. `json.loads("42")` is valid JSON, but not the object you wanted. After decoding, check the **shape**:

```python
if not isinstance(data, dict) or "id" not in data:
    raise ValueError("expected an object with an id")
```

For anything bigger, use a **validation** library such as Pydantic or `jsonschema`: you describe once what the data must contain, and it checks every input against that description. Or turn the dict into a **dataclass** (a simple class that just holds named fields) in one place. Either way, the rest of your code can trust what it gets.

Writing JSON can fail too: `TypeError` for unsupported types, and `ValueError` for NaN values when `allow_nan=False`, or for data that contains itself (a list that includes itself, for example).
concepts.code:
import json

def parse(text):
    try:
        data = json.loads(text)
    except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
        return f"line {e.lineno} col {e.colno}: {e.msg}"
    if not isinstance(data, dict) or not isinstance(data.get("id"), int):
        return "valid JSON, wrong shape"
    return data

print(parse('{"id": 1}'))            # {'id': 1}
print(parse(''))                     # line 1 col 1: Expecting value
print(parse('{"id": 1,}'))
# line 1 col 9: Illegal trailing comma before end of object
print(parse("{'id': 1}"))
# line 1 col 2: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes
print(parse('[1, 2]'))               # valid JSON, wrong shape
print(issubclass(json.JSONDecodeError, ValueError))  # True
takeaways: Catch `json.JSONDecodeError` (a ValueError) and report `lineno`/`colno`
Empty strings and HTML error pages are the most common culprits
Validate the decoded structure, not just the syntax
pitfalls: Catching every exception around a large block of code and printing a vague message, which hides the line and column that would explain the problem.

quiz.q: Your program downloads a reply from a web service, gets an empty string, and calls json.loads('') on it. What happens?
quiz.explain: An empty string contains no JSON value at all, so the parser fails at the very first character.

concepts.name: Serialising custom types with default
concepts.summary: Use the default= hook to write datetimes, Decimals, sets, dataclasses and other objects json can't handle on its own.
concepts.why: Real data contains dates and times, exact money amounts and your own classes, which json refuses out of the box.
concepts.body:
A **hook** is a function you hand to a library so the library calls your code at a certain moment. `json.dumps` has one called **default**. When it meets an object it doesn't know how to write, it calls `default` with that object. Your function must return something json can write (a str, number, list, dict...) or raise `TypeError` for types it doesn't handle either.

```python
def to_json(o):
    if isinstance(o, datetime):
        return o.isoformat()
    raise TypeError(f"{type(o).__name__} is not JSON serializable")
```

Typical conversions:

- `datetime`/`date` → `o.isoformat()`, an **ISO 8601** string: the international date format, like `2025-03-01T12:00:00`
- `Decimal` → `str(o)` to keep the exact digits (or `float` if precision doesn't matter)
- `set`/`frozenset` → `sorted(o)`, so the output is the same every time
- `UUID`, `Path` → `str(o)`
- dataclasses → `dataclasses.asdict(o)`, which converts dataclasses nested inside too
- `Enum` → `o.value`

Whatever `default` returns is then written the normal way. So if it returns a dict that contains other unusual objects, `default` is called again for each of them.

`default` is only called for types json can't handle. You can't use it to change how ints, strings or dicts are written. Objects of a class built on top of `dict`, `list`, `int`, `str` or `float` (a subclass of it) are written like the plain type, without calling it.

Reading doesn't undo this automatically: the datetime comes back as a string. Converting it back is the job of the reading side (the `object_hook` option of the next lesson, or a validation library).
takeaways: `default=fn` is called for each object json can't write; return something it can
Raise TypeError for types you don't handle
Reading gives back the strings; convert them back explicitly
pitfalls: Returning the object unchanged from `default`; json meets the same object again and fails with a 'Circular reference detected' error.

quiz.q: Which objects are passed to the default function during json.dumps(data, default=fn)?
options: Only values json cannot encode natively
quiz.explain: The encoder handles built-in JSON types itself and calls default only as a fallback.

concepts.name: Decoding into your own objects
concepts.summary: Customise decoding with object_hook, object_pairs_hook and parse_float to build objects, detect duplicates or keep exact decimals.
concepts.why: Turning raw dicts into your own objects as soon as the data arrives keeps the rest of the code simple.
concepts.body:
`json.loads` accepts **hooks**: functions you pass in, which json calls while it parses.

- **object_hook=fn** is called with every JSON object as soon as it has been read (as a dict), innermost first. Whatever it returns replaces that dict. Use it to turn tagged dicts into your own objects, e.g. `{"__type__": "point", "x": 1, "y": 2}` into a `Point`.
- **object_pairs_hook=fn** gets the object's contents as a list of `(key, value)` pairs instead of a dict. So it sees **duplicate keys**, which a dict would silently merge (the last one wins), and it's the way to reject them. If both hooks are given, this one wins.
- **parse_float=fn** is called with the text of every JSON number that has a decimal point. `parse_float=Decimal` keeps exact values like `"19.90"` for money.
- **parse_int=fn** does the same for whole numbers.
- **parse_constant** handles `NaN`, `Infinity` and `-Infinity`; raise an error there to reject them.

Hooks run on every nested object, so keep them fast, and make them return the dict unchanged when it isn't the kind they convert.

For more than a couple of types, converting after reading is often clearer: parse to plain dicts, then build your objects with ordinary code, or with a library that checks and converts data for you, such as Pydantic.
takeaways: `object_hook` transforms every decoded object, innermost first
`object_pairs_hook` sees raw key/value pairs, including duplicates
`parse_float=Decimal` keeps exact decimal values
pitfalls: Forgetting that hooks run for every nested object, so returning None for 'other' dicts wipes out data.

quiz.q: What does json.loads('{"k": 1, "k": 2}') return by default?
quiz.explain: Duplicate keys are allowed by the parser and the last value wins; object_pairs_hook can detect them.

concepts.name: JSONEncoder subclasses and iterencode
concepts.summary: Package custom JSON writing in a JSONEncoder subclass, and write large output in pieces with iterencode.
concepts.why: Some libraries ask for an encoder class (passed as cls=), and writing in pieces avoids building one huge string.
concepts.body:
**json.JSONEncoder** is the class that does the work behind `dumps`. Subclass it and override **default(self, o)** to get the same behaviour as the `default=` function, bundled with its options and reusable as `cls=`:

```python
json.dumps(data, cls=AppEncoder)
```

Some libraries take an encoder class rather than a function; the Django web framework's `JsonResponse`, for example. That's the main reason to prefer a subclass. In `default`, end with `super().default(o)`; the parent's version raises the usual `TypeError`.

`encoder.encode(obj)` returns the whole string at once, while **encoder.iterencode(obj)** hands it out in pieces, one after another. Writing each piece to a file or network connection as it comes means the whole document never has to sit in memory as one string. `json.dump` already uses `iterencode` when writing to a file.

Options such as `indent`, `sort_keys`, `ensure_ascii` and `check_circular` are arguments you pass when creating the encoder: `AppEncoder(indent=2)`.

You can't change how built-in types (`int`, `float`, `str`, `dict`) are written by overriding `default`. Overriding `encode` isn't enough either, because the **C accelerator** (a fast part of json written in the C language) writes nested values directly, without going through your Python method. If you need special float formatting, convert the values beforehand (for example, round them), or use a third-party library.

In the same way, `json.JSONDecoder` can be subclassed and passed as `cls=` to `loads`, mostly to bundle hooks together.
takeaways: Subclass `JSONEncoder` and override `default`; pass it as `cls=`
Finish `default` with `super().default(o)` to raise the usual TypeError
`iterencode` hands out pieces, so a huge document needn't be one string
pitfalls: Trying to change float formatting by overriding `default`; it is never called for floats.

quiz.q: Why might you write a JSONEncoder subclass instead of passing default=?
options: It is the only way to write datetimes
Some libraries accept an encoder class via cls=
quiz.explain: The behaviour is the same, but cls= is the option many libraries offer.

concepts.name: Large data and JSON Lines
concepts.summary: Handle big data one record at a time with JSON Lines, and read JSON values packed back to back with raw_decode.
concepts.why: Event histories, data exports and big collections of examples are often too large to load as one JSON document.
concepts.body:
`json.load` parses the whole document at once. So a 5 GB file holding one big array needs memory for the text plus all the resulting Python objects, often several times the file size.

**JSON Lines** (`.jsonl`, also called NDJSON) solves this with one JSON value per line:

```
{"id": 1, "event": "login"}
{"id": 2, "event": "logout"}
```

Each line is parsed on its own with `json.loads`. So you can read records one at a time, using the same small amount of memory however long the file gets. You can also add records to the end safely, and carry on past a bad line. Write each record with `json.dumps(record)` plus `"\n"`. The output of `dumps` never contains a real line break, because line breaks inside strings are written as `\n`. Don't use `indent` for JSON Lines.

Make readers forgiving: skip blank lines, and report the line number of broken ones instead of stopping a long job.

For text where JSON values follow each other without line breaks, the decoder class behind `loads` has a method for this: **JSONDecoder.raw_decode(s, idx)** parses one value starting at position `idx` and returns `(value, end_index)`. You can then walk through the string value by value.

For one truly huge document, such as one giant array, use a library that reads it bit by bit, like the third-party `ijson`. Or convert it once to JSON Lines, or to **Parquet**, a compact file format for tables that's built for data analysis.
takeaways: JSON Lines stores one JSON value per line: you can read it piece by piece and add to it
`json.dumps` output never contains a real line break, so it's safe for JSON Lines
`JSONDecoder.raw_decode` parses one value at a time from a string
pitfalls: Writing JSONL records with `indent=2`, which spreads each record across several lines.

quiz.q: Why can a JSON Lines file be read with a small, fixed amount of memory while one big JSON array cannot (with the standard library)?
options: Each line is a complete document that can be parsed and thrown away on its own
JSON Lines stores numbers in binary
quiz.explain: Reading line by line never needs more than one record in memory at a time.

concepts.name: Numbers, precision and NaN
concepts.summary: Understand how JSON numbers map to int, float and Decimal, why money needs care, and how NaN and Infinity are handled.
concepts.why: Silently losing digits in prices, IDs and measurements is one of the most expensive JSON bugs.
concepts.body:
JSON has a single number type with no limit on digits; how precisely to store them is left to each program. Python reads numbers without a decimal point or exponent as `int` (any size, exact) and the rest as `float`. A float is stored in a fixed 64 binary digits (64-bit), which keeps only about 15 to 17 significant digits.

Consequences:

- Decimal fractions are approximated: `0.1 + 0.2` is not `0.3`, and `"19.90"` reads as `19.9`. For money, read with `parse_float=Decimal` and write Decimals as strings, so no rounding happens.
- Python's big ints are exact. But in **JavaScript** (the language that runs inside web browsers) every number is a float. So integers above `2**53`, such as the long IDs some databases generate, lose their last digits in a browser. Web services often send such IDs as strings for that reason.
- `1.0` comes back as `1.0`, not `1`: a float stays a float.

**NaN and Infinity**: Python writes `float('nan')` as `NaN` and infinity as `Infinity`. JavaScript understands these words, but they are not valid JSON, and careful parsers reject them. Use `allow_nan=False` to raise `ValueError` instead, and turn such values into `null` yourself. When reading, Python accepts them by default; `parse_constant` lets you reject them.

`1e400` is too big for a float, so it is read as `inf`: an overflow quietly becomes `Infinity` too.
concepts.code:
import json
from decimal import Decimal

print(json.loads("[0.1, 19.90, 1.0]"))   # [0.1, 19.9, 1.0]
prices = json.loads('{"a": 0.1, "b": 0.2}', parse_float=Decimal)
print(prices["a"] + prices["b"])         # 0.3
print(json.loads("[0.1]")[0] + 0.2)      # 0.30000000000000004

big_id = 2**63 - 1
print(json.loads(json.dumps(big_id)) == big_id)   # True in Python
print(float(big_id) == big_id + 1)                # True: a JS float can't tell

print(json.dumps([float("nan"), float("inf")]))   # [NaN, Infinity]
try:
    json.dumps(float("nan"), allow_nan=False)
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)          # Out of range float values are not JSON compliant: nan
takeaways: JSON numbers become exact ints or approximate floats; use `parse_float=Decimal` for money
Integers above 2**53 lose digits in JavaScript programs; send big IDs as strings
`allow_nan=False` stops Python from writing invalid NaN/Infinity
pitfalls: Sending large 64-bit IDs as JSON numbers to a web page and getting the last digits rounded.

quiz.q: A Python web service sends {"id": 9007199254740993} (2**53 + 1). What does a JavaScript program typically see?
quiz.explain: JavaScript numbers are 64-bit floats, which cannot hold 2**53 + 1 exactly, so it is rounded to 2**53.

concepts.name: Parsing untrusted JSON safely
concepts.summary: Defend services against hostile JSON: size and depth limits, huge integers, duplicate keys and wrong types.
concepts.why: Any public web service that calls json.loads on data strangers send it is exposed to these attacks.
concepts.body:
`json.loads` is safe in one important way: it never runs code from the input (unlike `pickle` or `eval`). But hostile input can still hurt:

**Size**: a 1 GB message becomes several GB of Python objects. Limit how much data you accept before parsing; web servers and web frameworks have a setting for this.

**Depth**: `[[[[...]]]]` nested thousands of levels deep. The decoder protects itself from crashing and raises `RecursionError`, which is not a `ValueError`. So code that catches only `JSONDecodeError` lets it escape, and a web service answers with a "500 Internal Server Error". Catch it, or reject deeply nested input.

**Huge integers**: turning a number with hundreds of thousands of digits into an `int` takes time that grows with the square of its length. Since 3.11 (and security updates of older versions), **CPython**, the standard Python interpreter, refuses such conversions above 4300 digits by default and raises `ValueError`; `sys.set_int_max_str_digits` changes the limit. Pass `parse_int` to reject long numbers even earlier.

**Duplicate keys**: different JSON readers keep different values. Attackers use this to slip data past a check written in another language that saw the other value. Reject duplicates with `object_pairs_hook`.

**Wrong types**: `{"admin": "false"}` holds a non-empty string, so it is truthy. `{"ids": {"$gt": ""}}` passed into a database query can match every record, because some databases read `$gt` as "greater than". Check types strictly after decoding.

**NaN/Infinity**: accepted by default, they break comparisons and arithmetic. Reject them with `parse_constant`.
takeaways: json never runs code, but size, depth and huge numbers can still slow down or crash your service
Deep nesting raises RecursionError, not JSONDecodeError
Reject NaN, long integers and duplicate keys with parse hooks
pitfalls: Catching only JSONDecodeError around json.loads in a web service; RecursionError and other ValueErrors escape and crash the request.

quiz.q: A request body is '[' * 200000 + ']' * 200000. What does json.loads raise in CPython 3.13?
quiz.explain: The decoder's recursion guard raises RecursionError, which JSONDecodeError handlers don't catch.

concepts.name: Canonical JSON for hashing and signing
concepts.summary: Produce byte-identical JSON for equal data, so it can be fingerprinted with a hash, used as a cache key, or signed.
concepts.why: Fingerprints, cache keys and signatures break if the same data can be written as JSON in more than one way.
concepts.body:
Sometimes you need a fingerprint of some data: a **cryptographic hash** such as SHA-256, a short code computed from the exact bytes. Equal bytes always give the same fingerprint. You can use it to spot duplicates, as the name to store a cached result under, or together with a secret key to make a **digital signature** that proves who produced the data.

All of these work on bytes, and two equal dicts can produce different JSON text: key order follows the order keys were added, spacing depends on options, and non-ASCII characters may or may not be escaped. So anything that hashes or signs JSON needs **canonical JSON**: one fixed way of writing each piece of data.

A practical canonical encoding with the standard library:

```python
json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"), ensure_ascii=False).encode("utf-8")
```

That fixes the key order, removes optional spaces and fixes the text encoding. What's left for you to handle:

- **Floats**: Python writes the shortest form (`0.1`), but other languages may write `1e-7` differently from Python's `1e-07`. Avoid floats in data you sign; use strings or integers (cents, not dollars).
- **Accented letters**: `"é"` can be stored as one character or as `e` followed by a separate accent mark. Normalise with `unicodedata.normalize("NFC", s)` if text comes from different sources.
- **Types**: tuples and lists both become arrays; int keys become strings. Make data canonical after converting it to JSON's own types.
- **Sets**: sort them.

For agreement between languages there is a published internet standards document, RFC 8785 (JSON Canonicalization Scheme), which pins down number formatting exactly. For signing, sign the exact bytes you send and check the exact bytes you receive, rather than writing the data out again.
concepts.code:
import hashlib
import json

def canonical(obj):
    return json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"),
                      ensure_ascii=False).encode("utf-8")

a = {"user": "zoë", "roles": ["admin"], "id": 7}
b = {"id": 7, "roles": ["admin"], "user": "zoë"}

print(json.dumps(a) == json.dumps(b))          # False
print(canonical(a) == canonical(b))            # True
print(canonical(a))
# b'{"id":7,"roles":["admin"],"user":"zo\xc3\xab"}'
digest = hashlib.sha256(canonical(a)).hexdigest()
print(len(digest))                             # 64

print(json.dumps(1e-7))                        # 1e-07
takeaways: Use `sort_keys=True`, compact separators and a fixed encoding for canonical bytes
Floats and differently stored accented letters are remaining sources of difference
Sign or hash the exact bytes; RFC 8785 standardises canonical JSON
pitfalls: Hashing `json.dumps(obj)` with default options, so equal data built in a different order gets a different hash.

quiz.q: Which source of difference does sort_keys=True NOT remove?
options: Different float formatting in another language's encoder
Order of keys in nested objects
quiz.explain: Sorting fixes key order at every level, but number formatting still varies across implementations.

concepts.name: JSON performance and alternatives
concepts.summary: Know what makes the stdlib json fast or slow, and when to switch to orjson or msgspec.
concepts.why: Writing and reading JSON is often one of the slowest steps in web services and data pipelines.
concepts.body:
The json module is written in Python, with a **C accelerator** (`_json`) for reading strings and writing whole documents fast. Some calls skip the fast paths:

- `json.dump(obj, f)` writes in pieces through `iterencode`, which uses the slower Python encoder so it can hand out pieces. For documents that fit in memory, `f.write(json.dumps(obj))` is often several times faster.
- A `default` function or encoder subclass costs one Python call per unsupported object.
- Object hooks and `parse_float`/`parse_int` cost one Python call per decoded object or number.

Measure with `timeit` on realistic data before optimising. Often the bigger costs are around JSON: turning database records into dicts, or checking data with a slow validation library.

When JSON speed really matters, popular third-party libraries are several times faster:

- **orjson** (written in Rust, a fast compiled language) writes dataclasses, datetimes, UUIDs and NumPy arrays without help, and returns `bytes`.
- **msgspec** reads JSON and checks it straight into its own typed record classes ("structs") in one pass.
- **ujson** and **simdjson** bindings are other options.

They differ subtly from the standard library: orjson returns bytes, rejects NaN, and limits integers to 64 bits. Check these details before swapping.

For very large tables of data, compact formats that aren't text at all (binary formats), such as MessagePack, Protocol Buffers or Parquet, beat any JSON library.
concepts.code:
import io
import json
import timeit

payload = {"items": [{"id": i, "name": f"item{i}", "price": i * 1.5,
                      "tags": ["a", "b"]} for i in range(1000)]}

one_shot = timeit.timeit(lambda: io.StringIO().write(json.dumps(payload)), number=50)
streamed = timeit.timeit(lambda: json.dump(payload, io.StringIO()), number=50)
print(streamed > one_shot)         # True: dump streams via the Python encoder

text = json.dumps(payload)
plain = timeit.timeit(lambda: json.loads(text), number=50)
hooked = timeit.timeit(lambda: json.loads(text, object_hook=lambda d: d), number=50)
print(hooked > plain)              # True: one Python call per object

from json import decoder
print(decoder.scanstring.__module__)   # _json  (C accelerator in use)
takeaways: The standard json uses a C accelerator; streaming `dump`, hooks and `default` skip it
Measure realistic data before optimising
orjson and msgspec are much faster but behave differently with NaN, big integers and return types
pitfalls: Swapping in a faster library without checking how it handles NaN, big ints and return types.

quiz.q: A service writes a 50 MB response with json.dump(obj, f). Which change most likely speeds it up, memory permitting?
options: f.write(json.dumps(obj)), which encodes in one shot with the C encoder
quiz.explain: json.dump uses the chunked pure-Python iterencode; dumps encodes the whole object with the C fast path.
